text: So far, every customer attribute we've covered describes identity and terms. This lesson covers one that describes money: the bank account a customer pays from, or gets refunded to.

Most receipts just arrive, a wire or a check, and Receivables records that money came in. But two scenarios need the bank details on file in advance. Direct debit, where a customer authorizes the business to pull payment automatically near the due date. And refunds, where money owed back to the customer goes electronically to their account instead of a paper check.

Here's where it actually lives. A customer bank account is tied to the party, not to one specific account, so the same bank account can be authorized across more than one customer account belonging to that party. And before you can even enter it, the bank and branch themselves have to already exist as shared setup data, the same records Cash Management and Payables use. Receivables doesn't keep its own separate bank list.

Picture Cascade Outdoor Supply moving to automatic receipts. Their controller provides bank details once, Northwind confirms the bank and branch already exist in shared setup, and adds Cascade's account number tied to their party and authorized for the Cascade Outdoor Supply US account. From the next billing cycle, Northwind pulls each due invoice amount directly from that account on the due date. Up next, lesson eleven: merging and maintaining customers.
